compare_aerospace_diff: AeroSpace is keyboard-only and TOML-only: no settings UI, no focus ring, no bars, no mouse story. It also deliberately does not touch the native macOS Desktops — its workspaces replace them rather than working alongside them, so Mission Control and a Desktop-bound profile are not part of the model. KiwiDesk hides inactive windows exactly the way AeroSpace does, and adds the native Desktop layer on top of it.
compare_aerospace_good: Fast, SIP-clean and refreshingly opinionated. Its i3-style workspace model sidesteps macOS Spaces entirely, which makes it predictable in a way native Spaces rarely are, and its documentation is unusually good — good enough that our own docs send people to it.
compare_anchor_desktops_body: Being straight about this one: KiwiDesk’s own spaces are emulated by parking inactive windows off in a corner — the same technique {aero}AeroSpace documents{/aero}, and we cite them for it in our own docs. What is different is that KiwiDesk also drives the native macOS Desktops you already swipe between: send a window to Desktop 3, switch to it, and bind a profile to a Desktop so your whole setup loads when you arrive there. yabai reaches those operations through a scripting addition that needs SIP disabled. KiwiDesk {sip}never asks you to disable SIP{/sip}, and never will. And a window you want everywhere — a call, a notes panel, a calculator — can be made sticky so it follows you across every space, carrying a mark on the window itself and a badge on its Space Bar tile.
compare_anchor_desktops_title: Native macOS Desktops, without switching SIP off
compare_anchor_gui_body: yabai, AeroSpace and Rift are config-file-first by design: write a file, reload, repeat. That is a good model for people who enjoy it and a wall for everyone else. OmniWM ships a settings app too, though — so a GUI on its own is no longer what separates KiwiDesk, and this page is not going to pretend otherwise. What is different is what sits underneath it: KiwiDesk pairs its Settings app with a sandboxed Lua VM, a CLI and a JSON event stream, where OmniWM pairs its own with a TOML file. Everything — layouts, gaps, per-app rules, shortcuts, profiles — is reachable from either end, so the depth is something you reach for rather than the price of entry.
compare_anchor_gui_title: A Settings app with a scripting VM underneath
compare_anchor_mouse_body: yabai and AeroSpace are keyboard-first by design — AeroSpace has no mouse story at all — and for a lot of people that is the wall. KiwiDesk is built for both, though it is not alone in that: OmniWM has its own mouse resizing and trackpad gestures, and on this axis the two of us are comparable rather than one ahead. What KiwiDesk gives you is a window you drag across the desktop with live drop targets showing where it will land, a Space Bar you can drop that window onto to send it to another space, and a focus ring that tells you where the keyboard is in a dense layout. The App Bar and Space Bar are part of the app rather than a separate daemon to install and configure, and the shortcuts, modes and app-launch bindings are built in too — where yabai reaches for skhd.
compare_anchor_mouse_title: Built for the mouse as well as the keyboard
compare_anchor_permissions_body: KiwiDesk requests Accessibility and nothing else. No Input Monitoring: the hotkeys go through Carbon, so the permission that reads every keystroke is never asked for. No Screen Recording. And {sip}never SIP{/sip}. It also works whether macOS’s “Displays have separate Spaces” is on or off — {omni}OmniWM’s own README{/omni} requires it on and pauses window management until you enable it. Updates arrive in the app itself, so there is no brew upgrade habit to keep. The cost, stated plainly: without Input Monitoring, macOS’s own shortcuts win any conflict with yours — a trade we would make again, but a trade.
compare_anchor_permissions_title: It asks for as little as macOS allows
compare_anchor_tabs_body: Open a second tab in Finder, Safari or Ghostty and macOS quietly creates a second window — which is why tabs tend to spray stray tiles across a tiling layout. {ghostty}Ghostty’s own documentation{/ghostty} names this as a known issue for yabai and AeroSpace, and says the fix is not theirs to make: it is how the macOS window API works. Rift has it open as an issue of its own; OmniWM lists native-tab support among its features, though its docs do not describe the behaviour. KiwiDesk recognises the switch and keeps the tab group in one tile, with its float state and its place in the order intact. What it cannot do — and nor can anyone else — is split two tabs into two tiles: that would need cross-process window reparenting macOS does not permit, and we {limits}say so plainly{/limits} rather than leaving you to discover it.
compare_anchor_tabs_title: Native tabs do not scatter your layout
compare_cell_sip_yabai: Must be off for full features

compare_h1: KiwiDesk and the other macOS window managers
compare_intro: macOS has good window managers, and this page is not an argument that they are bad. It is here so you can work out quickly which one fits the way you work — including the cases where the answer is not KiwiDesk.
compare_intro_honesty: Everything here was checked against each project’s own documentation, and the claims that turn on a source link to it — including ours. Where we could not verify something, this page says so rather than guessing.
compare_magnet_diff: Magnet snaps windows into regions; it does not manage a layout. There is no automatic tiling when a window opens, no spaces model, no per-app rules, no profiles that reshape the whole desktop, and no scripting. It is also paid and closed source. If what you want is “Magnet, but it keeps arranging things for me”, that is roughly the gap KiwiDesk fills.
compare_magnet_good: The one most Mac users have actually heard of, and deservedly so: it costs a few euros, you understand it in thirty seconds, and dragging a window to a screen edge solves the problem most people actually have. Rectangle does much the same thing for free.
compare_meta_desc: An honest comparison of KiwiDesk with yabai, AeroSpace, Rift, OmniWM and Magnet: what each one does well, which permissions each asks for, and where KiwiDesk is genuinely different.
compare_meta_title: KiwiDesk vs yabai, AeroSpace, Rift, OmniWM and Magnet — macOS window managers
compare_nudge_dev_short: Compare with yabai, AeroSpace and Rift
compare_omniwm_diff: Two differences worth knowing before you choose. It requires Input Monitoring at launch, where KiwiDesk asks only for Accessibility; and it requires macOS’s “Displays have separate Spaces” to be on, pausing window management until it is, where KiwiDesk works either way. Underneath its GUI is a TOML file rather than a scripting VM, it ships two layouts to our seven, and it is GPL-2.0 where KiwiDesk is MIT — which matters if you intend to reuse the code.
compare_omniwm_good: The closest thing here to a peer: Swift, SIP-clean, notarized builds, and the only other one in this list with a real settings app. Its niri-style scrolling and dwindle BSP layouts are well made, and it has grown fast.
compare_outro: Free and MIT-licensed, for macOS 14 and later on Apple silicon. Arriving from one of the tools above? The {lua}Lua reference{/lua} shows how far the configuration actually goes.
compare_pick_aerospace: if you want a fast, keyboard-only, i3-style workflow, and you would rather replace macOS Spaces than work with them.
compare_pick_kiwidesk: if you want real tiling without writing a config file first — a Settings app, a mouse that works, focus rings and bars built in, native Desktop and profile binding with SIP on, and Lua underneath for when you outgrow the GUI.
compare_pick_magnet: if you just want to snap a window to half the screen and never think about it again.
compare_pick_omniwm: if you want a Swift, SIP-clean window manager with a settings app and niri-style scrolling, and neither Input Monitoring nor the separate-Spaces requirement bothers you.
compare_pick_rift: if you want a modern Rust config-file window manager with scrolling columns and its own overview, and a young project does not put you off.
compare_pick_title: So which one should you use?
compare_pick_yabai: if you want to script your window manager deeply, you are at home in a shell config, and you accept the SIP trade-off for its full feature set.
compare_rift_diff: Rift is configured through a TOML file with no settings app, and its on-screen surface is a menu bar item rather than focus rings and bars. It is also young and moving quickly, which cuts both ways: features land fast, and things change. We could not find documentation of how it handles native macOS tabs, so this page makes no claim about that in either direction.
compare_rift_good: The newest of these and the most technically ambitious: written in Rust, SIP-clean, with five layouts including niri-style scrolling columns, trackpad gestures and its own Mission Control-style overview. If you want a fast, modern, config-file window manager, it is a serious option.

compare_yabai_diff: Two differences. Its fuller feature set — moving windows between Spaces, opacity, window sub-levels — needs the {sip}scripting addition, which requires partially disabling System Integrity Protection{/sip}; KiwiDesk reaches Desktop operations through a bridge that works with SIP on, and simply does not offer the parts that would need SIP off. And yabai is configured by editing a shell script, with no settings UI at all. Where yabai is genuinely ahead of us: its ecosystem, and the sheer volume of published configurations to copy from. It has a five-year head start and it shows.
compare_yabai_good: The most capable and most scriptable window manager on macOS, with by far the deepest community. Its query API and signals are the reason so much of the macOS ricing ecosystem — SketchyBar, JankyBorders, skhd — grew up around it. If you want to program your window manager, yabai is still the reference.

guide_faq_1_a: No. The Settings app covers everything — layouts, gaps, monitors, shortcuts, app rules — all with clicks and sliders. Lua is there for tinkerers who want to script their setup, but it's entirely optional. Most people never open a config file.
guide_faq_1_q: Do I need to know Lua or write any code?
guide_faq_2_a: No — it works alongside them. KiwiDesk arranges the windows inside its own Spaces; your macOS Desktops and Mission Control keep working just as they do now. You can even assign a different setup to each Mission Control Desktop, so it switches automatically as you move between them.
guide_faq_2_q: Does it replace Mission Control or macOS Desktops?
guide_faq_3_a: Yes. KiwiDesk runs entirely on your Mac, as an ordinary app with no kernel extension. It only moves and resizes windows — it never reads your files, and it isn't a keylogger (its shortcuts use a built-in macOS mechanism, not keyboard monitoring). It never asks you to weaken your Mac's built-in protections.
guide_faq_4_a: KiwiDesk is a small, native macOS app built to sit quietly in the background. It only does work when your windows actually change, and its animations run at each display's own natural refresh rate. Day to day, you shouldn't notice it in the background at all. If you'd rather have no animation at all, one switch in Colors & Animations turns off every window animation at once, and KiwiDesk already honors Reduce Motion if that's on in your System Settings.
guide_faq_4_q: Will it slow down my Mac or drain the battery?
guide_faq_5_a: Quit KiwiDesk from its menu-bar icon and remove the app like any other. If you installed it with Homebrew, run brew uninstall --cask kiwidesk. The moment it's off, your windows behave exactly like normal macOS windows again — free to drag, resize, and overlap. Nothing sticks, and nothing of yours was ever changed.
guide_fav_callout_p: Nothing here is permanent. Switch layouts as often as you like — there's no wrong choice, and you can always go back. KiwiDesk only ever moves and resizes windows; it never touches your files or your apps.
guide_fav_callout_title: It's okay to change your mind
guide_fav_p1: The best way to find your layout is to try a few and feel which one suits your day. Open the Settings window from KiwiDesk's menu-bar icon, go to Layout, and pick a mode for the Space you're on. Your windows rearrange right away, so you can see each one live — switch, look, switch again.
guide_fav_p2: When one feels right, it's already saved for that Space. You can even give different Spaces different layouts: a focused stack for writing, a wide scrolling row for research, whatever fits.
guide_gs_a11y: Using VoiceOver or the keyboard? Settings announces every control by name and value, and you can reach all of it without a mouse — the user guide has the details, including the one macOS setting you need to turn on.

guide_isit_p: If you spend even a little of your day dragging windows around, you'll probably feel the difference. A few everyday moments, before and after:
guide_keys_bonus: Bonus points if you can drive KiwiDesk one-handed afterwards — then you've always got a hand free for your next kiwi. 🥝
guide_keys_callout_p: Worst case, something doesn't work the way you meant for a minute. KiwiDesk doesn't break anything and never touches your files — it just moves windows around. So experiment.
guide_keys_note_1: ⌃⌥ (Control-Option) is the quiet corner. macOS barely uses it and most apps don't touch it at all — which is why the defaults live there.
guide_keys_note_2: ⌥ (Option) on its own types characters. On a US keyboard ⌥L is ¬ and ⌥5 is ∞. Adding ⌃ or ⌘ stops that.
guide_keys_note_3: ⌥⌘ (Option-Command) with arrows is tab switching in most browsers and terminals. Those have no menu to fall back on, so they're the ones people miss most when they go.
guide_keys_notes_sub: A few things I kept in mind
guide_keys_p1: Thanks for being here. Genuinely — wanting the keys to fit you better is the whole idea. The nearer they get to your own habits, the more this stops feeling like a tool you operate and starts feeling like your Mac just works the way you want it to.
guide_keys_p2: What ships is a starting point I chose to be easy to pick up without walking over macOS and your usual apps, but you know your hands and your habits better than I do. Below are a few things I kept in mind — I don't follow all of them myself, so take the ones that matter to you and skip the rest.
guide_keys_search: Really want to be sure? Most apps publish a full list — search for <app name> keyboard shortcuts.
guide_keys_try_1: Think about where you actually use shortcuts — the two or three apps you live in, and the macOS ones you'd notice losing.
guide_keys_try_2: Bind it, then open that app once and see whether anything behaves differently.
guide_keys_try_3: If something does, come back and change it. Nothing here is permanent, and you can always reset to the defaults.
guide_keys_warning: KiwiDesk tells you when macOS itself already owns a chord, and shows it on the keyboard preview. It can't see what your other apps use, though — which is what step 2 is for.
guide_layout_bsp: Windows split the screen into tidy panes, each new one halving the pane it lands in. Balanced, edge to edge.
guide_layout_floating: The plain macOS way: windows float freely, right where you drag them. KiwiDesk leaves these ones alone.
guide_layout_grid: Everything laid out in even rows and columns — see all your windows at once, each with its own equal square.
guide_layout_monocle: One window fills the screen while the others wait quietly behind it. Pure focus, no distractions.
guide_layout_scrolling: Windows sit side by side in one long row, like frames on a filmstrip — the focused one always front and center.
guide_layout_stack: One big window holds your focus, with the rest lined up neatly beside it — glance over.
guide_layout_track: Side-by-side columns (or rows), each holding as many windows as you like — one column per task or project.
guide_layouts_p: A “layout” is just the shape your windows arrange themselves into. KiwiDesk has seven. You don't have to learn them all — most people find one they like and stay there. Here's each, in plain language.

guide_settings_p: Everything is point-and-click — you never need to edit a file. Open Settings from the KiwiDesk menu in your menu bar. A sidebar on the left groups things into Design (the look and feel of the profile you're working on) and System (settings that apply everywhere). Here's what each section is for.
guide_title: A calmer Mac, in a few minutes
guide_tour_apprules_body: Automatically send an app to a chosen Space every time you open it, keep certain windows floating, and pick the Settings language — all point-and-click.
guide_tour_bars_body: Two optional on-screen strips. The Space Bar shows all your Spaces at a glance — click one to jump there, or drag a window onto it to send it over. The App Bar lists every window in the monocle and scrolling layouts, so nothing hides; click a tab to focus it, or drag tabs to reorder. Little badges mark windows that float or stay pinned everywhere.
guide_tour_behavior_body: Adjust how things feel: what dragging a window's edge does, whether the pointer follows your focus, where new windows appear, and how KiwiDesk tidies your windows into a reachable grid if you ever quit it.
guide_tour_colors_body: Pick a whole color set in one click — every palette shows a small scene painted in its own colors, so you can see the look before you take it, and the scene underneath shows the colors you're running right now. Applying a palette paints once; you're free to change any single color afterwards. Animation lives here too: whether windows animate at all, which moments they animate, and how long each glide takes. And if you ever do want one specific color rather than a whole set, Advanced Colors sits right below with all 25 of them, grouped by where you see them on screen — most people never open it.
guide_tour_gapsborders_body: Set the breathing room between your windows, and the shape of the small visuals — the soft highlight that shows where a window will land as you drag it, the ring around the window you're focused on, and whether a window pinned everywhere carries a little mark. Sizes and shapes here; the colors have a section of their own.
guide_tour_layout_body: Pick a layout for each Space and tune how it behaves. This is where you choose your favorite arrangement — and, if you like, give one Space its own tweaks without changing the rest.
guide_tour_monitors_body: Have more than one display? Pin a Space to a screen by dragging it onto that monitor. Handy when you dock and undock.
guide_tour_profiles_body: Save a whole setup as a profile and switch between them — one for focused work, another for a second screen at your desk.
guide_tour_shortcuts_body: See and change the keyboard shortcuts, recorded by simply pressing the keys you want. Every conflict is flagged for you.
guide_tour_spaces_body: Name the Spaces you use — “web”, “mail”, a number — and KiwiDesk keeps each one tidy on its own.

quote_cli: The day my window manager became scriptable, my desktop started running itself. I haven't dragged a window since.
quote_cta: They say an apple a day — but the kiwi's got more vitamins and bigger plans... 🥝
quote_demo: Fair warning: it's about as oddly satisfying as watching kiwis stack kiwis. You'll open windows on purpose, just to watch them snap into place.
quote_dev: Even though I'm perfectly comfortable in the terminal, I got tired of having to constantly track container nesting just to arrange my windows the way I want. KiwiDesk keeps everything flat. No unnecessary overhead, no distractions: just pure focus on my projects.
quote_opening: Tiling managers were always a nerd's toy. I wanted to make them intuitive for everyone – it should just work, like that.
quote_simple: I built KiwiDesk because I wanted to show my friends how good it feels to never tidy your windows again — calm, effortless, and honestly kind of fun.
quote_tagline: I wanted a window manager that works with you — not one you have to tell how to work.
what_body: KiwiDesk is a window manager: it puts your open windows in order for you, instead of leaving that to you. Open a window and it slots neatly into place beside the others — tidy, edge to edge, no gaps you didn’t ask for.
